en: The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Gateways of Boundless Birth.
By the Marquis of Suo, who holds the rank of Kaifu Yitong Sisi and serves as Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
with an appanage of three thousand households, invested with purple robes and posthumously honored as Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, Tripitaka Master of the Great Xingshan Monastery, who was posthumously titled Dajian and formally named Daguangzhi, by imperial decree. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling in the Multi-storied Pavilion of the Great Forest at Vaiśālī.
Together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
the World-Honored One, at that time, through his mindfulness and perfected wisdom, knew that I had relinquished the life-process.
"Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately commanded the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana to go to the trichiliocosm.
He announced to all the bhikṣus,
"Assemble all together at the multi-storied pavilion in the Great Forest.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it; we shall follow your instructions.
Then, in a single kṣaṇa, by means of his own supernormal power, he reached the summit of Mount Sumeru and uttered a great sound.
Proclaim throughout the great trichiliocosm:
"Listen all of you! Within this world, the Buddha’s disciple, the Great Master, shall now let fall the rain of Dharma. May all who desire to hear it assemble here."
At that time, forty thousand bhikṣus all assembled at the multi-storied pavilion in the Great Forest.
Having seen the World-Honored One, these bhikṣus...
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, had this thought:
"I should now manifest a supernatural power of such a kind."
Having manifested and performed these supernormal powers,
[he reaches] even those dwelling within the trichiliocosm,
whether they belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Great Vehicle.
"I shall cause them all to assemble in the Great Forest Multi-storied Pavilion.
At that time, Śāriputra immediately manifested such supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). By means of this manifestation of supernormal power, [he accomplished his purpose].
Even those dwelling throughout the trichiliocosm—
whether followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna—
all gathered together at the Great Forest Multi-storied Pavilion.
Having all come to see the World-Honored One,
they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Namely, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati,
the Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva,
and the Bodhisattva Apāyajaha.
The Bodhisattva Chanderamśa (Severing the Darkness of Sorrow),
the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin (Remover of All Obstructions),
the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha (Luminous Net), and the Bodhisattva Sarvaviṣayajñānavinivartana (Wisdom that Extinguishes All Objects).
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, and Gandhahastin Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Vīramati,
the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
and the Bodhisattva Amitaprabha.
The Bodhisattva Candraprabha,
the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla,
and the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati,
the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha,
and the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
Prajñākūṭa Bodhisattva,
and Maitreya Bodhisattva.
"You all should go to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and summon the bodhisattvas in their final body,
the bodhisattvas in their last birth before buddhahood, the non-regressive bodhisattvas, those who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, or those with faith and understanding."
They all assembled in the Great Forest Multi-storied Pavilion; immediately those bodhisattvas, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, replied, “So be it, World-Honored One.”
In that very instant, he manifested such a supernatural realm;
by means of this supernatural realm,
within the multi-storied pavilion of the Great Forest, he...
Inexpressible times inexpressible hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas in their final bodies all gathered there.
Furthermore, there were ninety koṭis of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of bodhisattvas in their last birth before enlightenment (ekajātipratibaddha).
They all gathered together.
Furthermore, three hundred thousand nayutas of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas all came to gather.
Additionally, thirty koṭis of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of bodhisattvas who had attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas all came to gather.
Furthermore, there were eight hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who possessed faith and understanding;
all such bodhisattvas gathered together.
Having come to see the World-Honored One, they bowed their heads at his feet in salutation.
Having circumambulated the Buddha three times, they withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing the assembly of great bodhisattvas,
immediately had this thought:
I shall inquire about such principles from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
by hearing such an appropriate explanation and prophecy regarding these principles,
[I shall understand] them for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
They shall sever all doubts and swiftly attain unimpeded eloquence and wisdom;
throughout Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
they shall hear the essential teachings of the Tathāgatas.
Having heard them, they shall all receive and uphold them until they attain unsurpassed bodhi;
during that interval, they shall remember and maintain the essential teachings they have heard without forgetting them.
Bodhisattvas have four dharmas of pure conduct.
What are these four? They are:
purity of sentient beings, purity of dharmas, purity of vows, and purity of the merit that adorns the Buddha-field.
Having attained those dharmas,
there are four kinds of pleasing dharmas:
pleasure of body, pleasure of speech, pleasure of mind, and the arising of joy.
Having attained those dharmas,
one is able to enter the four gates of dhāraṇī. What are the four?
That is to say: the dharani-door of entering the inexhaustible arising and ceasing;
the dharani-door of skillfulness regarding the faculties of sentient beings;
and the dharani-door of skillfulness regarding karmic retribution and the unconditioned.
Entering the dhāraṇī gate of the profound dharma-patience,
Śāriputra then contemplated this principle as previously described and explained it in detail for the World-Honored One.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the essential principles of the Dharma as taught by you,
so that Bodhisattvas may attain purity through their practice.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon them.
Having spoken thus, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
You are able to take pity upon many people and have compassion for their peace and happiness."
It is for the benefit and happiness of many, including gods and humans,
that you are able to inquire about such a meaning.
You should listen well, listen very well, and reflect with focused mindfulness.
"I shall explain it for you.
Having heard this from the Buddha, Śāriputra replied, "So be it, World-Honored One; we pray that you will proclaim it for us."
Then the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all dharmas,
should neither grasp nor cling to them, and should thus receive and uphold these words of the mantra-dhāraṇī."

Bhaṭṭe (73), Anācchane (74), Dhāraṇi (75), Dharmanidhāna (76), Traile (77), Samantapāśvare (78), Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhāna (79).
*Dṛṣṭe svāhā.* Having spoken this dhāraṇī, he addressed Śāriputra:
When upholding this dhāraṇī, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not conceptualize conditioned or unconditioned phenomena;
they do not apprehend them, do not disparage them, and do not abandon them.
Neither grasping nor manifesting;
regarding what has been attained, they do not give rise to superimposition concerning abandonment or cultivation;
they neither act, nor refrain from acting, nor engage in active manifestation.
One does not see the conjunction of phenomena, nor the dispersal of phenomena;
one does not see the arising of phenomena, nor the cessation of past phenomena;
one does not see the increase or decrease of future or present phenomena.
One does not designate dharmas as beneficial or non-beneficial; rather,
one should simply practice the recollection of the Buddha-samādhi,
which, at the time of cultivation, is neither form nor formless.
Neither signless nor non-signless;
neither possessing the secondary marks nor lacking the secondary marks;
neither consciousness nor non-consciousness.
Neither affliction nor non-affliction;
neither precept nor non-precept;
neither samādhi nor non-samādhi.
There is no wisdom, nor is there non-wisdom;
there is no liberation, nor is there non-liberation;
there is no knowledge and vision of liberation.
It is not that there is no knowledge and vision of liberation;
it is neither birth nor non-birth;
it is neither lineage nor non-lineage.
Neither having retinues nor lacking retinues;
neither abiding nor not abiding;
neither attainment nor non-attainment.
It is neither manifest realization nor non-manifest realization;
it is neither the exhaustion of afflictions nor the non-exhaustion of afflictions;
it is neither the aggregates, elements, and sense bases nor the absence of aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom;
neither teaching the Dharma nor not teaching the Dharma;
neither self-purification nor purification by another.
It is neither the purification of sentient beings nor the absence of the purification of sentient beings;
it is neither self-benefit nor benefit for others;
it is neither the Dharma nor discipline.
It is not purity of body, nor purity of speech;
it is not purity of mind, nor purity of conduct;
it is not purity of past conduct, nor purity of future conduct.
It is not a purification of conduct in the present life;
it is neither one's own form nor another's form.
Śāriputra, such is this bodhisattva.
Entering into the ineffability of all phenomena,
the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) is the equality of all phenomena;
it is named the fearless dhāraṇī that sustains the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
It is named the Samādhi of the Certainty of All Intents Being Perfectly Fulfilled.
It is the accumulation of all roots of goodness and wisdom;
it is the lineage of the Dharma-treasury, attained not through the power of another, and endowed with the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence.
It is called the *dhāraṇī* of supreme skill in seeking against Māra, which cannot be insulted or humiliated by others;
it is also called the *dhāraṇī* that transcends all demonic activities.
Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva attains the meaning of this *dhāraṇī* of the Gate of Boundless Emergence, [they shall be so empowered].
They shall attain non-retrogression and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
Regarding this treasury of all the merits of the Buddha-dharma,
one will certainly also attain the distinctions of all bodhisattva practices through the *animitta-dhāraṇī*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Seeking nothing within empty dharmas, Not engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding bodhi,
And remaining unmoved within the dharma-realm— Then one attains dhāraṇī.
One should listen to this sutra, the *Akṣayadhāraṇī*;
through it, wisdom is accomplished, and from this, one realizes bodhi.
By upholding this dhāraṇī, the bodhisattva attains fearlessness.
Having heard the supreme Dharma from the Buddhas of the ten directions,
one is able to understand that sublime and wondrous teaching; its meanings and phrasing are in perfect accord,
like the radiance of the sun, and the attainment of its words and meanings is likewise so.
Having attained the sublime Dharma, all vast dhāraṇīs will manifest before them; by virtue of upholding this sūtra,
even those sentient beings who remain throughout the kalpa and pose difficult questions [will be benefited].
They have all severed their doubts; their wisdom is inexhaustible.
As the eldest son of the Dharma King, they have drawn near to supreme enlightenment and been entrusted with the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings, because of their love for this sutra.
Sentient beings all love and delight in it, and the Buddhas likewise show compassion for it;
its fame pervades the world. By upholding this dhāraṇī, eighty koṭis of Buddhas will appear at the time of one's death.
By extending a hand to receive that person, through the upholding of this dhāraṇī,
all the various karmic offenses committed during a thousand koṭis of kalpas will be purified within a single month;
this is by virtue of upholding the dhāraṇī.
The mass of merit accumulated by a Bodhisattva over ten million eons is surpassed in a single month by one who upholds this dhāraṇī;
for even if all sentient beings in the three realms were to become Māras, [they could not overcome them].
They shall be unable to create obstacles or hindrances; by virtue of upholding this sutra,
their mindfulness, conduct, and wisdom will become supreme, and they shall possess the power of retention such that it constantly turns upon the tip of their tongues until they realize enlightenment.
As it is said in this sutra, one will certainly attain dhāraṇī;
the Tathāgata has declared herein that through this, one attains bodhi.
By hearing this dhāraṇī, Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me the prediction of enlightenment.
In a single instant, one beholds Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
if one wishes to know all those Buddhas and all the teachings they have proclaimed,
one should study this sutra, and all shall be swiftly attained.
The Buddha-fields shall be purified; the śrāvakas shall attain accomplishment, and all their marks of radiance shall be pure. This sutra can bring about all these things;
one should practice without negligence and contemplate it for seven days.
Eighty koṭis of Buddhas have bestowed this dhāraṇī:
One should not think that which is to be thought; Do not think what is not to be thought, and be careful not to think;
That which is to be thought should not be thought— Then one will obtain the dhāraṇī.
Just as one who enters the great ocean does not seek various treasures, yet obtains them;
so too, by obtaining this dhāraṇī, one does not seek other forms of peace and happiness, yet draws near to perfect enlightenment. Therefore, you should practice it.
Having attained the state of tranquility, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas."
Having attained this dhāraṇī, what are the four? They are as follows:
namely, non-attachment to sensual desire.
He harbors no envy toward any sentient beings.
He gives away all his own wealth and possessions with a heart free from regret.
Day and night, he loves the Dharma and finds delight in the Dharma itself.
"Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains dhāraṇī by accomplishing four dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
One should abandon the foul and impure desires, the wretched realm of Māra;
for through these one falls into hell and they become the cause for rebirth in the evil destinies.
Do not harbor envy toward others for the sake of kinship, fame, or profit.
Beholding sentient beings with eyes of loving-kindness, one attains great majesty and wondrous form.
Since the disputes and litigations of sentient beings have the accumulation [of possessions] as their root, one should therefore abandon greed; by relinquishing greed, one attains dhāraṇī.
Day and night he seeks the Dharma with single-minded devotion to attain the *bodhi-dhāraṇī*.
Through the practice of such a sūtra as this,
furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva—
One attains dhāraṇī by accomplishing four dharmas.
What are these four? They are:
practicing in an araṇya, a place of extreme non-contention.
Abiding in the power of profound patience regarding the Dharma,
they do not cling to gain, honor, or fame,
nor to any objects of affection.
One gives in charity without looking back with attachment,
even regarding one's own body and life.
Śāriputra, by accomplishing these four dharmas, [one attains this].
He immediately attained dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"One should dwell in an araṇya, as praised by the Buddha; Dwelling there, one should not disparage others."
One should delight in the patience regarding the most profound Dharma, Exerting oneself with diligence as if one’s head were on fire.

Do not give rise to greedy attachment for profit; For such causes and conditions, one becomes hypocritical in conduct, Coarse yet content like a bird, Attaining the fruit of being born in a human body.
How marvelous! To have well-attained the Dharma of the Tathāgata— One should abandon the household, the root of much suffering, and purify one’s body, speech, and mind.
Those who crave gain and profit lack mindfulness and wisdom; They have no faith, no precepts, and no reflection upon the Dharma.
Enlightenment is as remote as empty space; therefore, one should remain far removed from craving and attachment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes four dharmas attains this dhāraṇī.
What are the four? They are the entry into the meaning of the eight syllables. What are the eight?
That is to say:
the syllable BA is the ultimate truth;
it enters into the selflessness of all phenomena.
The syllable *la* refers to the marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*), as well as the absence of marks and secondary characteristics;
thus, it enters into the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Tathāgatas.
The syllable *va* refers to the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of noble ones.
Entering accordingly into non-duality and non-distinction:
the syllable *ja* signifies that birth, old age, and death are neither birth, old age, and death, nor do they go away;
one enters accordingly into the unborn and the unceasing.
The syllable KA represents karmic maturation and that which enters into what is not karmic maturation.
The syllable DHĀ represents the essential dhāraṇī of the Dharma: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Entering into accordance with the dharma-realm.
The syllable ŚA signifies śamatha and vipaśyanā;
it is neither śamatha nor vipaśyanā, for all dharmas are such.
Entering into True Suchness (tathatā):
The syllable *kṣa* signifies that all phenomena are momentary, inexhaustible, indestructible, bodiless, and fundamentally quiescent;
thus, one enters into the nirvāṇa of all phenomena.
One should accordingly enter into the meaning of these eight syllables;
this is the entry into the primary meaning within this essential dharma of the dhāraṇī.
One should skillfully transcribe it and uphold it;
this immediately accords with the second meaning within this essential dharma of the dhāraṇī.
Every half-month, one should read this with diligent practice and focused mindfulness;
thus, one will enter the third meaning within this essential dharma of the dhāraṇī.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices this should exhort, console, and praise all sentient beings,
causing them to train in and study this dhāraṇī.
Thus, one enters the fourth meaning.
Śāriputra, by means of these four dharmas, a bodhisattva mahāsattva achieves them and attains this dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke in verse:
"Contemplate the meaning of these eight words; Transcribe and uphold this sutra, And for half a month, you should read and practice it.
Furthermore, you should exhort other sentient beings [to do the same]."
Approaching the vast wisdom of enlightenment, he perceives directly all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions where the Buddhas abide; from them he has studied and learned faith—
Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Those who cultivate this dhāraṇī shall obtain four kinds of merit.
What are these four?
It is said that all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, will universally receive and protect one;
there shall be no demonic obstacles,
and karmic hindrances will be swiftly removed.
Śāriputra, by practicing this dhāraṇī, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains unimpeded eloquence.
One attains four kinds of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"All Buddhas embrace and protect them; the hosts of Māra find no opportunity."
Karmic obstacles are swiftly removed, and unimpeded eloquence is attained.
Śāriputra, in the distant past, beyond countless, more than countless, vast, sublime, and immeasurable kalpas ago.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Ratnaśrītejorāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world during the aeon [known as] Ratnaśrītejorāja.
The One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Leader, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, at the time when the Tathāgata King of Jewel-Auspicious-Majestic-Light entered parinirvāṇa in that kalpa,
There was a human king named King Dhṛtaprabha, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who possessed the seven treasures.
That king had a son.
His name was Inconceivable Merit Jewel Auspiciousness (*Acintyaguṇaratnaśrī*).
At the age of sixteen,
he heard from that Buddha this essential dharma of the *Dhāraṇī of the Emergence of Boundless Gates* (*Anantamukhasamudgata-dhāraṇī*).
As soon as he heard this dhāraṇī, he dwelt with diligent application for seventy thousand years without ever sleeping;
he was not greedy for royal power, nor for his own life or wealth.
For seventy thousand years, he remained in constant meditative silence, never resting his side upon the ground;
at the abodes of ninety million *koṭi* Buddhas,
he heard and received the True Dharma.
Having heard it, they all mastered it through total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
They then attended upon that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaśrītejo-rāja during the *kalpa* [known as] Ratnaśrītejo-rāja,
and there, in the presence of that Buddha, they went forth into homelessness.
After ninety thousand years have passed,
one will accomplish this "Dhāraṇī of the Gate of Boundless Emergence.
Once it has been accomplished,
He extensively expounded it for the sake of all sentient beings. Thus,
within a single lifetime, he established eighty quadrillion nayutas of sentient beings in unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He attained the stage of non-retrogression. Śāriputra, within that assembly,
there was a son of a householder named Candrasūryadhvaja.
Having heard this "Dhāraṇī of the Gateways to Boundless Emanation" from the Dharma-preaching bhikṣu,
he gave rise to profound sympathetic joy.
By virtue of these roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy,
he heard the True Dharma from ninety thousand koṭis of Buddhas;
having heard it, he retained it all entirely through dhāraṇī.
Thus, one becomes a possessor of the supreme dhāraṇī,
a speaker of the most excellent and dignified speech,
and one endowed with the most excellent and uninterrupted eloquence.
Those many Buddhas were served with reverence for three *kalpas*.
After those three *kalpas*, they realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra, there may be those who are hesitant, who give rise to doubt, or whose wisdom is otherwise.
At that other time, the elder’s son Candradhvaja should not have viewed it in such a way. Why is this?
Because at that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was the elder’s son Candradhvaja.
Śāriputra, there may be those of hesitant mind who give rise to doubt and divergent views;
at that future time,
as for that Dharma Master Auspiciousness of the Jewel of Inconceivable Virtue—
One should not view it in such a way.
Why? Because at that time, the Tathāgata Amitāyus was the Dharma Master Maṅgalaketu, whose merit was inconceivable.
Śāriputra, we bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of this Bhadrakalpa, having heard this sutra,
have given rise to deep sympathetic joy. By virtue of these roots of goodness born from sympathetic joy, [we shall attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment].
Having cast behind them forty koṭis of kalpas of wandering in birth and death,
they heard the True Dharma from ninety thousand koṭis of Buddhas and all became possessors of supreme dhāraṇīs.
He is the one with the most excellent and sublime speech;
he is the one with the most excellent and uninterrupted eloquence.
Therefore, Śāriputra, those who wish to swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices even with sympathetic joy toward this Dharma,
why is it that such a bodhisattva attains the stage of non-retrogression?
Serving a Dharma teacher serves as a cause for unsurpassed bodhi;
how much more so is it to copy, receive, uphold, read, and recite [the teachings].
Reflecting with right mindfulness, one explains this to others;
the measure of this mass of merit cannot be known by any sentient being except for the Tathāgata.
It is unknowable and inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Having heard this sutra, one gives rise to sympathetic joy; One copies it, receives and upholds it, and recites it."
All sentient beings cannot fathom it; The flow of merit continues without interruption.

In every birth they behold all Buddhas, Attaining pure faith and inconceivable understanding, Thoroughly comprehending the profound sutras and their principles, And swiftly awakening to supreme Bodhi.
He does not lose his samādhi, nor does he lose his supernormal powers or dhāraṇīs;
he does not lose his physical form, wealth, or the sight of the Buddhas.
Until he realizes unsurpassed enlightenment, I recall that in a former life long ago, he was the son of an elder who heard this dhāraṇī.
We have personally beheld Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; we rejoice in their awakening to great Bodhi.
In a former life, Dīpaṃkara was the son of an elder;
in a previous birth, Amitāyus was a Dharma teacher. We all rejoice in these Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Those who desire to swiftly realize awakening, Who wish to swiftly crush all māras,
And who aspire to be adorned with the marks of a hundred merits— For them, this application will not be difficult to attain.
Even if worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges Were all filled with the seven precious jewels and offered as gifts, [it would still be surpassed].
The merit derived from writing and upholding [this text] is such that even the merit of giving and making offerings does not approach it.
Therefore, having heard this, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence.
For the wise Bodhisattva who receives, upholds, writes out, and contemplates this dhāraṇī, I say that awakening will not be difficult to attain.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding this *Anantamukha-saṃbhava-dhāraṇī*,
there are eight great yakṣas who dwell in the Snowy Mountains and attend upon the bodhisattva mahāsattva engaged in its preparatory application.
They all come to augment the body of the practitioner,
providing empowerment and protection day and night.
What are these eight?
The first is named Śūra Yakṣa, translated into Chinese as "Valiant";
the second is named Nṛtya Yakṣa, translated as "Firm";
and the third is named Prabhūta Yakṣa, translated as "Sovereign."
The fourth is named Nārāyaṇamala Yakṣa (translated into Chinese as "Nārāyaṇa Power");
the fifth is named Cītramatī Yakṣa (translated into Chinese as "Wisdom in Action").
Sixth is the yakṣa named Nudaśa, translated into Chinese as "Difficult to Subdue" (Nàcuī).
Seventh is the yakṣa named Kaṇara, translated into Chinese as "Growling" (Héngzhī).
Eighth is the yakṣa named Sumaha, translated into Chinese as "Wondrous Arm" (Miàobì).
When they all arrive, the practitioner should bathe and put on fresh, clean robes.
They should practice walking meditation (caṅkrama) regardless of body or life.
They should give rise to a mind of great compassion that pervades all sentient beings.
One should recite this dhāraṇī;
those eight great yakṣas will swiftly manifest themselves to the practitioner.
At each gate, there are eight great bodhisattvas.
Those born in the heavens of the desire realm also come to empower and sustain them.
What are these eight?
They are the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu, the Bodhisattva Prajñāprabha,
the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha,
and the Bodhisattva Vibodhana.
The Bodhisattva Paripūrṇasarvāśaya,
the Bodhisattva Jyotiṣprabharāja,
and the Bodhisattva Caritaprajña.
Those eight bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained dhāraṇī and abide in the application of practice while cultivating dhāraṇī;
they are bodhisattvas engaged in application.
Abiding in reality and maintaining faith;
knowing and repaying kindness while loving and delighting in the Buddha-dharma;
and abiding in profound dharma-patience.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who cultivates dhāraṇīs and practices the sūtras should cultivate equanimity toward both material wealth and the Dharma,
even when giving away the slightest gift.
If one is still able to practice it with equanimity even toward a single person, how much more so toward many?
When the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī, [the earth shook in six ways.]
Thirty nayutas of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of thirty Ganges Rivers,
by obtaining this *anantamukha-saṃbhava-dhāraṇī*,
attained non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
One hundred and sixty *bimbara* of humans and devas,
who had not previously resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is the name of this sutra?
I shall receive and uphold it."
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "For this reason,
this sutra is named 'The Birth of Boundless Gateways.
You should receive and uphold it."
It is also called "The Definitive Attainment of Sarvajñā-jñāna";
you should uphold it. It is also called "The Definitive Birth of Bodhisattvas"; you should uphold it.
It is also called "The Destruction of the Hosts of Māra.
You should receive and uphold it. When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, [the assembly rejoiced and practiced accordingly].
The Venerable Śāriputra, along with the great bodhisattvas, devas, asuras, gandharvas, and others,
were all greatly rejoiced;
they received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
